tytul: Kombucha with black and green tea (NCHFP recipe)
wstep: This card describes the NCHFP kombucha recipe, made with black and green tea, sugar and a SCOBY, and kept in the refrigerator after fermentation.

akapity: Before you start, the pH of the starter liquid must be 4.0 or less; if it is greater than 4.0, do not make kombucha with that starter.
Do not use glazed ceramic (earthenware) containers for fermenting or storing kombucha, because the acidic drink can leach heavy metals.
Storing kombucha in airtight containers builds up carbon dioxide and can lead to an explosion if it is not checked regularly.
NCHFP uses 1 gallon of water, divided, 3 tablespoons (or 6 tea bags) of black tea and 1/3 cup plus 2 tablespoons (or 13 tea bags) of green tea.
It also uses 1 cup of granulated sugar and 1 SCOBY with its starter liquid.

Guidelines for producers from the New York State Department of Agriculture and Markets say to use a commercially purchased culture (SCOBY) for the first batch; later batches may be started from earlier ones only if they show no mold or unusual contamination.
No washing, boiling or other treatment removes lead from ceramics, and a poorly fired glaze can release lead into food and drinks.
Clean the kitchen area and wash your hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds.
Wash and rinse the equipment, then submerge it in hot water of at least 171 °F (about 78 °C) for at least 30 seconds to sanitize it.
Put 1 tablespoon of the starter liquid in a small bowl and test it with a pH strip or litmus paper, following the test paper maker’s instructions.
If the pH is 4.0 or less, continue, and discard the sample you tested.
If the pH is greater than 4.0, do not make kombucha with this starter liquid.
Heat 4 cups of the water to 160–170 °F (about 71–77 °C), checking it with a food thermometer, and steep the tea for 2 minutes.
Remove or strain the tea, pour it into the fermentation container, add the sugar and stir until it dissolves.
Add 12 cups of cold water.
The tea must be below 95 °F (35 °C) before you add the SCOBY and starter liquid.
Add the SCOBY and starter liquid and stir well for 10 seconds.
Dry the opening of the container and cover it with a paper towel, coffee filter or clean cheese cloth, secured with a rubber band or string.
Mark the container with the date; this is day 0 of fermentation.
Ferment the kombucha at room temperature, 68–77 °F (20–25 °C), for 7–10 days.
The recommended pH of finished kombucha is between 2.5 and 4.2.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): on day 7, test the pH of the kombucha with a pH strip, as NCHFP describes for the starter liquid.
If the kombucha does not reach a pH of 4.2 or lower within 7 days, the culture is probably contaminated or the temperature too low, and the batch should be discarded.
Fermenting for more than 10 days can raise the acidity of kombucha to a potentially harmful level.
When fermentation is complete, pour the kombucha into clean, sanitized jars or bottles, refrigerate it promptly and use it within 30 days.

If you mix other ingredients into kombucha after fermentation, drink it immediately or keep it in the refrigerator for up to 2 days; the NCHFP recipe does not cover a second fermentation in a closed bottle.
Under some conditions the alcohol content can exceed 0.5% by volume, the US TTB limit for a non-alcoholic drink.
Dry, fuzzy spots, white or colored, on the SCOBY or on the surface of the kombucha mean that it has spoiled; discard both the drink and the SCOBY.
UGA Extension considers up to 4 fluid ounces (about 120 ml) of kombucha a day safe for most healthy people.
UGA Extension does not recommend kombucha for people prone to acidosis, people with weakened immunity, or pregnant or breastfeeding women.
